content.thinking: Since there's no metrics data or root cause identified, I should write an honest postmortem that openly acknowledges what remains unknown rather than fabricating certainty.

assumptions: That the alert itself was accurate is assumed, not verified — with no metrics retrieved, we have no independent confirmation that error rates were in fact elevated.
The start of impact is assumed to be the moment the alert fired; no actual onset time could be measured, so the real problem may have begun earlier.
Any duration or impact figure derived from this incident is a lower bound only: the service had not recovered by the last minute of data available, so the true extent is unmeasured.
The absence of recent feature-flag changes is taken from the flag provider's history; other classes of change (deploys, dependency or infrastructure changes) were not checked and are not ruled out.
input.executive_summary: An automated alert reported an elevated rate of failed requests in one of our services starting at 18:36 UTC on 26 September 2026. The automated responder picked the incident up immediately, attempted to pull the service's recent performance data, and got nothing back — the data needed to confirm what was happening, how many users were affected, or how bad it was could not be read. It also checked whether any recent configuration change might explain the problem and found none. With no evidence to work from, it handed the incident to on-call engineers about a second after the alert arrived. At the point our records end the service had not recovered, so the problem was still ongoing and its full duration and customer impact are unknown. No fix was applied by the automated responder; the outcome depends on the human response that followed, which is outside this record.
input.root_cause: Not determined. The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop fired at 18:36:16Z, but the investigation returned zero minutes of metrics for the incident window and the flag provider showed no recent configuration changes, so no candidate cause could be supported by evidence; the incident was escalated to humans roughly one second later with the fault still active and unexplained.
